prompt:
Please turn each photo I upload into an individual high-end architectural observation poster, no multi-image stitching, output each photo separately.

Prefer a 4:3 horizontal side-by-side composition. The left side occupies about 50%, faithfully preserving the original photo; the right side occupies about 50%, reinterpreting the same scene as an "ink-line and color architectural observation drawing."

The boundary between the left and right areas must be straight, clear, and cleanly cut. Do not fade, feather, tear paper, atomize, or permeate each other, and do not let photos, ink lines, plants, or color blocks cross the boundary. The boundary itself does not need extra line work.

The left side preserves the subject identity, architectural structure, topographical relationship, spatial direction, natural light and shadow, real texture, and original color atmosphere of the original photo, with only slight, restrained high-end photographic color grading to give it the texture of architectural magazines, museum publications, and art exhibition photography. Do not stretch, distort, move, replace, or redesign the subject.

The right side uses warm off-white natural paper as a background, observing and extracting the most recognizable architectural motifs from the photo, such as roofs, eaves, doorways, columns, platforms, walls, steps, railings, corridors, and primary spatial directions, reorganizing them into a modern Eastern paper-based architectural observation drawing.

Do not duplicate the photo completely, nor draw all the architectural details. Use one or two irregular ink shapes in deep black or gray-black to establish the main architectural outline and visual weight, such as using a solid mass of ink to generalize a roof, eave, or wall; then use a small number of thin, slightly broken gray-black ink lines to suggest columns, railings, perspective directions, and necessary structural nodes.

Follow: 
Overall architectural main shape > spatial direction > necessary structure > tiny details.

Tiles, window lattices, brick patterns, carvings, brackets, and railings should not be depicted precisely one by one. Complex structures should be actively deleted, merged, and generalized so that the original building can be identified at a glance, while retaining traces of manual observation, on-site sketching, and artistic reduction.

Do not depict plants leaf by leaf. Compress tree canopies, bamboo forests, shrubs, and distant vegetation into a few irregular dots and dry-brush color blocks of gray-green, moss green, sage green, olive green, or ochre. Trunks and branches should only be suggested with a very few dark lines.

If the photo contains water, represent it only with a few sets of intermittent, sparse gray-blue or gray-green horizontal strokes; do not fill the entire water area. Sky, air, ground, mist, and distance can be represented directly by the unpainted paper whitespace.

The right side should retain at least 40% to 60% continuous paper whitespace. All ink shapes, lines, and colors should be grouped around a main architectural motif; do not distribute fragmented strokes evenly across the paper, and do not fill the background to explain the complete environment.

Extract the color scheme from the original photo, but compress it into a restrained limited palette. Dominated by ink black, gray-black, warm gray, gray-green, moss green, mineral blue-green, ochre, and off-white, retaining only one small area of warm color as a visual focus.

If the original photo contains an important person, they can be kept as the only small area vermilion silhouette; if there is no person, do not add one. Recognizable red columns, lanterns, door panels, or signature components from the photo can also serve as the single vermilion focus, but do not let multiple warm elements compete for attention.

Use real paper painting texture: 
bold black ink mass, broken line sketch, handmade observational aesthetics, large artistic negative space.
